name: Trifarotene (Aklief)

card.summary: Aklief is an Rx RAR-gamma-selective retinoid cream approved in 2019 for acne on the face and trunk; large vehicle-controlled trials back it, and no anti-aging approval exists.
card.note: Prescription-only. Irritation, dryness and sunburn are the most common adverse reactions; pregnancy data are limited.

quick.overview:
Trifarotene (Aklief) is a prescription topical retinoid from Galderma, approved by the US FDA in October 2019 for acne vulgaris in people aged 9 and older [2][3]. It is described as a first-in-class, fourth-generation retinoid that selectively targets the retinoic acid receptor gamma (RAR-gamma) [2][6].

Its main distinction is that the pivotal studies enrolled people with acne on both the face and the trunk, giving it rigorous clinical data on truncal acne that other topical retinoids lack [4][6]. Later phase 4 trials have looked at post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation and atrophic acne scars [9][11].
quick.mechanism: Trifarotene is an agonist of retinoic acid receptors with particular activity at the gamma subtype, the most common isoform in skin [3][6]. Like other topical retinoids, it increases keratinocyte differentiation and reduces proliferation, which lowers hyperkeratinization, and may reduce inflammation [6]. The label states that the exact process by which it improves acne is unknown [3].
quick.risks: The most common adverse reactions (1% or more) are application-site irritation, itching and sunburn [3]. The label advises moisturizer, reduced frequency if needed, and sun protection [3]. Available trial data have not identified a pregnancy-related risk, but case reports with other topical retinoids describe birth defects similar to those from oral retinoids [3].

lead: Trifarotene, sold as Aklief (a 0.005% cream), is a topical retinoid developed by Galderma that selectively activates retinoic acid receptor gamma (RAR-gamma) and is classed as a fourth-generation retinoid [2][1]. The US FDA approved it in October 2019 for the topical treatment of acne vulgaris in patients 9 years of age and older [2][3].

Its distinguishing feature is clinical data on truncal acne. Reviewers state that, unlike earlier topical retinoids, it is the first with rigorous trial data on safety and efficacy for acne on the trunk as well as the face [6][4]. It is approved for acne only; it does not carry an anti-aging indication, and Grokipedia notes limited clinical evidence for anti-aging use [3][1].
In looksmaxxing forums, trifarotene appears mostly as a prescription step between tretinoin and isotretinoin for acne, discussed by teenagers and young adults [18].

paras: The label indication is topical treatment of acne vulgaris in patients aged 9 and older [3]. Guidelines from the American Academy of Dermatology make a strong recommendation for topical retinoids in acne in general [7]. A 2026 European update of the EuroGuiDerm guideline prioritised a question on which patients should receive new topical treatments such as trifarotene and clascoterone [8]. Trifarotene is also described as having received an orphan designation for congenital ichthyosis, with a phase 2 ichthyosis study in the registry, but it is not approved for that condition [19][1].

Pivotal trials. Two phase 3, double-blind, randomized, vehicle-controlled 12-week studies of once-daily trifarotene 50 micrograms per gram cream enrolled participants aged 9 and older with moderate facial and truncal acne; primary endpoints were Investigator's Global Assessment success on the face (clear or almost clear with at least a 2-grade improvement) and changes in inflammatory and non-inflammatory lesion counts, with truncal success as a secondary endpoint [4]. One of the two registered studies enrolled 1,208 participants [16]. A review summarising these data describes trifarotene as efficacious in reducing comedones and papules/pustules, and as safe and well tolerated [6].
Long-term data. A long-term study (registered with 453 participants) and its published report examined safety and efficacy over a longer duration in moderate facial and truncal acne [5][17].

Hyperpigmentation and scars. A phase 4 trial (LEAP) in acne-induced post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation in skin of color, run with a skincare routine including UV protection, was published in 2024, and a later qualitative interview study reported that trifarotene-treated patients in this trial had faster improvement in hyperpigmentation than those on vehicle cream at week 12 [9][10]. A phase 4 controlled study reported that trifarotene reduced the risk of atrophic acne scars [11].

Comparisons. A trial of tazarotene 0.045% lotion compared its irritation potential with adapalene 0.3% gel and trifarotene 0.005% cream in two studies [12]. Narrative reviews place trifarotene among newer acne therapies alongside clascoterone and sarecycline [20][15]. Registered studies compare a trifarotene 0.005% cream with Aklief [21].
Cosmetic and anti-aging outcomes. No studies found of trifarotene for photoaging or wrinkles in the sources reviewed.

The most common adverse reactions (1% or more) are application-site irritation, application-site itching and sunburn [3]. Warnings cover skin irritation (erythema, scaling, dryness, stinging or burning), for which the label suggests a moisturizer from the start and reduced frequency if needed, and ultraviolet exposure, where the label advises minimizing sunlight and using sunscreen and protective clothing [3].

Pregnancy. The label notes that clinical-trial pregnancies did not identify a risk of major birth defects or miscarriage, but that case reports exist of birth defects similar to those after oral retinoids in women exposed to other topical retinoids; it states these do not establish a pattern [3]. Animal studies with oral doses are discussed in the label [3].

The label describes trifarotene as an RAR agonist with particular activity at the gamma subtype, which modulates genes involved in cell differentiation and inflammation, and states that the exact process by which it improves acne is unknown [3]. RAR-gamma is the most common RAR isoform in skin, and the selectivity is said to account for efficacy at low concentration [6]. Its design from a structure-based approach, aimed at making a RAR-gamma-selective agonist with a wider safety margin than earlier RAR-beta/gamma retinoids, was reported in 2018 [14]. Nonclinical and human pharmacology data and a clinical pharmacology and safety report have been published [13][22].

Galderma Research and Development developed trifarotene, and it received its first global approval in the USA in October 2019 [2]. Reviews describe a lineage of topical retinoids from tretinoin (FDA-approved 1971) through successive generations to RAR-gamma-selective agents [15].

On looksmax.org, a young poster says their dermatologist recommended Aklief as a last resort before isotretinoin after tretinoin did not work, and that they chose it partly because of concerns about isotretinoin's effects on growth; replies include support for the choice and a comment that most topical retinoids are "cope" for long-term remission [18]. The poster's claims about isotretinoin are the poster's own and are not assessed in this article.

timeline.event: FDA approves tretinoin, the first topical retinoid for acne [15].
Pivotal phase 3 and long-term safety studies of trifarotene begin [16][17].
Phase 3 results published; FDA approves Aklief for acne in patients 9 and older [4][2].
Phase 4 study on atrophic acne scars published [11].
Phase 4 study in acne-induced post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation in skin of color published [9].

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, Aklief appears in acne threads as a prescription option short of isotretinoin, especially among younger posters [18].

claims.claim: Aklief is a reasonable step before isotretinoin when tretinoin has not worked
claims.believers: One poster says their dermatologist offered it as a last resort before isotretinoin and that it is "working pretty good so far" for them [18].
claims.experts: AAD guidelines strongly recommend topical retinoids for acne and recommend oral isotretinoin for severe acne, acne causing psychosocial burden or scarring, or acne failing standard oral or topical therapy [7].

claims.claim: Trifarotene works on face and body acne
claims.believers: Forum posts describe it as treating acne and scarring on the face and body [18].
claims.experts: Phase 3 trials enrolled people with facial and truncal acne, and reviews state it has rigorous trunk data [4][6].

claims.claim: Topical retinoids are not enough for long-term remission
claims.believers: A reply says most topical retinoids are "cope" for long-term remission [18].
claims.experts: A long-term safety and efficacy study of trifarotene has been published, and guidelines recommend combining topical therapies with different mechanisms [5][7].

claims.claim: Aklief carries no significant systemic absorption concerns
claims.believers: The poster says it acts on the face and body without significant systemic absorption [18].
claims.experts: A clinical pharmacology and safety study of trifarotene has been published, and the label discusses pregnancy and animal data; Grokipedia reports very low plasma concentrations [22][3][1].
